blocks.title: Why Building Golden Datasets matters in a real product

spans.text: Problem statement:

A team is dealing with a support bot needs a trusted set of examples that catches policy and citation mistakes. They do not need trivia about Building Golden Datasets; they need a decision they can make, a concrete artifact they can inspect, and a way to know whether coverage of top user intents and edge cases is improving.

This lesson keeps one running case in view: golden dataset card with inputs, expected outputs, and rubrics. Every module asks what the system sees, what it changes, what can go wrong, and how a reviewer would prove the behavior before trusting it.

Before reading on, predict: if the dataset mirrors yesterday's easy demos and misses current failures, which part of the design would you inspect first - input, mechanism, decision rule, implementation, or monitoring?
Because this is an intermediate lesson, assume the vocabulary is learnable and spend your effort on tradeoffs, integration points, and the tests that prove the design works.

items.text: Business framing: Building Golden Datasets matters when it changes a launch, buy/build, safety, or quality decision for the product team.
Engineering framing: Building Golden Datasets matters when it changes state, interfaces, tests, traces, data, model behavior, or runtime limits.
Validation framing: the lesson is not done until coverage of top user intents and edge cases can be measured on examples that look like the real workload.

blocks.title: Fully worked example: golden dataset card with inputs, expected outputs, and rubrics

spans.text: Scenario: a support bot needs a trusted set of examples that catches policy and citation mistakes. The team wants coverage of top user intents and edge cases, but it has already seen the failure mode where the dataset mirrors yesterday's easy demos and misses current failures.
Here is the worked artifact at the level you would bring to a design review.
Complete artifact

items.text: User-facing goal: deliver a reliable Building Golden Datasets experience for the running case, not a demo that only works on easy examples.
Inputs: one realistic user request, the available evidence or data, and any policy, schema, budget, or latency constraint that limits the answer.
Decision rule: choose the smallest design that can satisfy the goal and expose the failure signal. If the evidence is missing or risky, stop or escalate instead of guessing.
Output contract: return the answer, decision, or artifact plus the evidence used, the confidence or pass/fail status, and the next action for a reviewer.

Verification: run at least three cases - happy path, ambiguous edge case, and the known failure case: the dataset mirrors yesterday's easy demos and misses current failures. Track coverage of top user intents and edge cases before and after the change.

spans.text: A complete prompt/checklist you could hand to an AI assistant

Role: You are helping build or review golden dataset card with inputs, expected outputs, and rubrics. Context: the product case is a support bot needs a trusted set of examples that catches policy and citation mistakes. Task: produce a one-page plan that states the input contract, processing steps, output contract, validation cases, and owner for each risk. Constraints: do not invent evidence; call out missing data; prefer the smallest testable design; include the failure case "the dataset mirrors yesterday's easy demos and misses current failures". Output schema: {goal, inputs, steps, validation_cases, risk_owner, metric}.
That is the standard to copy throughout the lesson: concrete scenario first, full artifact second, then mechanism, tradeoff, code or verification, and solo application.

blocks.title: Mechanism: the applied idea

spans.text: Mechanism is the part of Building Golden Datasets that explains why the running system behaves the way it does. For a support bot needs a trusted set of examples that catches policy and citation mistakes, do not start by naming tools. Start by tracing the path from input to decision to output.
Plain-language framing
Imagine the system as an operations checklist. A request arrives, the system gathers evidence, a rule or model transforms that evidence, and the result must be checked before anyone relies on it.
Engineering framing

Now translate the same flow into contracts: input schema, state carried between steps, external calls, model or algorithm decision, validation result, and logged evidence. The contract is what lets you debug the dataset mirrors yesterday's easy demos and misses current failures.
Recall from module 1: the running artifact is golden dataset card with inputs, expected outputs, and rubrics. Which field in that artifact would expose coverage of top user intents and edge cases?

blocks.title: Case study: the first review meeting

spans.text: The team reviews golden dataset card with inputs, expected outputs, and rubrics after a week of prototype use. One user-visible metric is improving: coverage of top user intents and edge cases. But a reviewer finds the known failure pattern: the dataset mirrors yesterday's easy demos and misses current failures.

The decision is not to throw away the prototype. The team keeps the working slice, then adds one missing control: better state capture, stricter retrieval, a clearer schema, a human approval step, or a monitoring alert depending on the failure.

items.text: What changed: the artifact now records the evidence it used, not just the final answer.
What stayed small: the team did not optimize the entire stack before proving the failure could be detected.
What got measured: coverage of top user intents and edge cases became part of the release gate, not an after-the-fact dashboard.

blocks.title: Design choices: the applied idea

spans.text: The design choice is rarely "use Building Golden Datasets" or "do not use it." The real choice is how much rigor to add for this user's risk, data, and operational burden.

In the running case, a thin slice is useful only if it proves the hardest assumption. Production design is justified when users depend on the behavior. Advanced optimization comes later, after traces show the bottleneck or failure pattern.

items.text: Choose the thin slice when the requirement is still uncertain and you need fast feedback.
Choose the production path when the failure would affect users, money, compliance, or trust.
Choose advanced optimization only after measured evidence shows the baseline is the limiting factor.

blocks.title: How this breaks in practice

spans.text: The happy path for Building Golden Datasets is not enough. In the running case, watch for failures that look successful until a user, auditor, or downstream system checks the details.

items.text: Silent success: the system returns an answer or artifact but hides that evidence was missing, stale, or incomplete.
Wrong abstraction: the team optimizes a model, framework, or metric when the real problem is data quality, policy, state, or workflow ownership.
Evaluation gap: tests cover polished examples but not the known failure case: the dataset mirrors yesterday's easy demos and misses current failures.
Operational drift: the design works once, then degrades when traffic, data, users, or dependencies change.

spans.text: Specific diagnostic: when coverage of top user intents and edge cases worsens, inspect the first step where evidence enters the system and the last step where the output is validated.

blocks.useWhen: Use the production path when a support bot needs a trusted set of examples that catches policy and citation mistakes affects real users and coverage of top user intents and edge cases is part of launch quality.
blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid advanced optimization while the team still cannot reproduce or detect the failure where the dataset mirrors yesterday's easy demos and misses current failures.
blocks.ruleOfThumb: First make the failure visible, then make the system faster, cheaper, or more sophisticated.

blocks.title: Runnable check: turn a golden case into a release gate
blocks.code:
# Building Golden Datasets: minimal eval gate.
golden = {
    "id": "refund-policy-1",
    "must_include": ["30 days", "invoice id"],
    "must_not_include": ["guaranteed approval"],
}
answer = "Refund requests need the invoice id and must arrive within 30 days."

def passes(case, answer):
    lower = answer.lower()
    has_required = all(term.lower() in lower for term in case["must_include"])
    avoids_forbidden = all(term.lower() not in lower for term in case["must_not_include"])
    return has_required and avoids_forbidden

print(golden["id"])
print("pass" if passes(golden, answer) else "fail")

spans.text: This is not the full production implementation of Building Golden Datasets. It is a runnable miniature that makes the lesson's contract visible: input, decision, output, and a check tied to the running failure mode.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Predict the eval result before revealing. Does this candidate pass the tiny golden case?

It prints:
refund-policy-1
pass

The answer includes both required facts and avoids the forbidden over-promise. A real harness would add many cases and richer assertions, but the gate shape is already visible.

questions.why: The lesson is valuable only if it changes an artifact, release gate, or evaluation tied to coverage of top user intents and edge cases.
questions.rot: Prefer the smallest design that exposes the failure case: the dataset mirrors yesterday's easy demos and misses current failures.

spans.text: From memory, reconstruct Building Golden Datasets as a five-part path: the concrete problem (a support bot needs a trusted set of examples that catches policy and citation mistakes), the mechanism, the design choice, the implementation or verification check, and the failure mode (the dataset mirrors yesterday's easy demos and misses current failures). Then name the metric that tells you whether the work improved: coverage of top user intents and edge cases.
